stem: A 68-year-old woman comes to the office due to recurrent episodes of syncope and intermittent dizziness.  The episodes usually occur after getting up from a chair or out of bed.  She has hypertension and chronic kidney disease and takes lisinopril and clonidine daily.  Blood pressure is 155/85 mm Hg, and pulse is 44/min.  One of her medications is discontinued, and the syncopal episodes resolve.  The drug responsible for this patient's symptoms most likely functions through which of the following mechanisms?​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​

explanation:
Medication-induced orthostasis

Mechanism

Examples

α1 blockade–mediated vasodilation

  • Terazosin, prazosin, doxazosin
  • Antipsychotics (eg, risperidone, quetiapine)
  • Antihistamines, TCAs

Other vasodilation

  • ACE inhibitors & ARBs
  • Dihydropyridine CCBs
  • Hydralazine, nitrates
  • Phosphodiesterase inhibitors

Volume depletion

  • Diuretics
  • SGLT-2 inhibitors

Sympathetic blockade

  • β blockers
  • Clonidine

ARBs = angiotensin II receptor blockers; CCBs = calcium channel blockers;SGLT-2 = sodium-glucose cotransporter-2; TCAs = tricyclic antidepressants.

This patient's syncopal episodes are most likely due to bradycardia and decreased peripheral vascular resistance caused by clonidine.  Clonidine is used in the treatment of severe or refractory hypertension.  It exerts its effects on both heart rate and blood pressure by stimulating presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic receptors in the rostral ventrolateral medulla (area responsible for basal and reflex control of sympathetic activity).  This effect results in a subsequent decrease in postganglionic release of norepinephrine and decreased sympathetic outflow, causing both bradycardia and a decrease in peripheral vascular resistance.

Normally upon standing, a baroreceptor-mediated increase in sympathetic drive causes vasoconstriction (to increase peripheral resistance) and increased heart rate and contractility (to aid cardiac output).  These changes facilitate a corrective increase in blood pressure to prevent a drop in cerebral perfusion.  However, when this normal response is impaired (eg, attenuated sympathetic outflow from clonidine), cerebral perfusion can decrease and lightheadedness or syncope can result.

Lisinopril may also contribute to orthostatic syncope by impairing peripheral vasoconstriction, but the effects are less profound than those of clonidine because heart rate is not inhibited.

(Choice A)  Beta blockers (eg, atenolol) block beta-1 adrenoreceptors in the sinoatrial node (and atrioventricular node), which can lead to bradycardia and contribute to orthostatic syncope.  Clonidine does not block adrenoreceptors; it reduces central sympathetic output.

(Choice B)  Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (eg, diltiazem, verapamil) block calcium channels in the atrioventricular node and myocardium, resulting in slowed AV nodal conduction, decreased heart rate, and decreased contractility that can contribute to orthostatic syncope.  Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (eg, amlodipine) can contribute to orthostatic syncope via peripheral vasodilation.

(Choice C)  Class III antiarrhythmics (eg, dofetilide) bind to and block the potassium channels responsible for phase 3 repolarization of the cardiac action potential.  This effect does not contribute to orthostatic syncope, but it can prolong the QT interval and increase the risk of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (ie, torsade de pointes), a serious cause of cardiac syncope.

(Choice D)  Postganglionic parasympathetic neurons release acetylcholine.  Decreased acetylcholine release would reduce parasympathetic activity and tend to increase heart rate, rather than cause the marked bradycardia seen in this patient.

Educational objective:Clonidine, an antihypertensive agent, stimulates central alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, causing a decrease in postganglionic release of norepinephrine and reduced sympathetic outflow.  This attenuates the normal baroreceptor-mediated increase in peripheral vascular resistance and heart rate during standing and can cause orthostatic syncope.​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​
